opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say the FOMO is quite high right now, though it's not evenly spread. It's concentrated at the top. If you look at the foundation model companies and a handful of well-known application teams, valuations are being set less by fundamentals and more by the fear that if you miss this round, you'll never get in. Many investors have internalized the lesson from the mobile internet era that the winners capture almost everything, so they'd rather overpay for a seat at the table than be left out.

At the same time, there's a quieter part of the market where things are much more rational, maybe even too cautious. Early teams that don't have a famous founder or a flashy demo are finding it harder to raise money than people assume. So it's a polarized market: extreme enthusiasm for a small number of names, and a fair amount of hesitation for everyone else.

Part of what drives the FOMO is genuine uncertainty. Nobody really knows where the value will settle. Will it go to the model layer, the infrastructure layer, or the applications? When you don't know, the instinct is to spread bets across all the obvious candidates, and that pushes prices up for the consensus picks.

My own view is that some of this will look irrational in hindsight. The technology is real and the long-term impact is probably being underestimated, but the timing and the distribution of returns are another matter. Historically, transformative technologies have created enormous value while many of the early investors still lost money. So I'd say the FOMO is understandable, but investors should separate "this technology matters" from "this particular deal at this price makes sense." Those are very different questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses high, polarized FOMO and investors spreading bets across likely candidates, but does not say they sound one another out to obtain information.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the FOMO is real, but it's also a bit more nuanced than people assume from the outside.

If you look at the primary market right now, the capital is extremely concentrated. There's a very small group of foundation model companies and a handful of infrastructure plays that are absorbing most of the money, and for those deals the FOMO is intense. Valuations get set less by what the company has built and more by who else is in the round and how scarce the allocation is. I've seen rounds close in days, with investors doing very little diligence because they're afraid that if they ask too many questions, they'll just be cut out. That part is unmistakably bubbly.

But outside of that top tier, the picture is actually quite different. For application-layer companies, for teams working on narrower vertical problems, fundraising is not easy at all. Investors are asking hard questions about moats, about whether the business survives the next model release, about whether they're just a thin wrapper. So you have this strange split where a few companies can raise at almost any price and everyone else is being told to show revenue.

My own view is that FOMO in this cycle is partly rational. Investors look at mobile internet and remember that if you missed the two or three platform companies, you basically missed the decade. So they're willing to overpay for the chance to be in the right room. The problem is that this logic only works if the winners are already identifiable, and I don't think they are. The technology is still moving too fast, and the cost structure of these companies is unlike anything we've seen before. You're writing checks into businesses that burn capital on compute at a scale no software company ever has.

So if I had to summarize: at the top, FOMO is high and it's distorting prices. In the middle and the long tail, it's actually fairly disciplined, maybe even too cautious. And the real risk isn't that people are excited, it's that the excitement is pulling capital toward a very small number of bets, which means the entire market's outcome depends on whether those specific bets pay off.

r001.rationale: The response describes investors tracking who else is in a round and doing little diligence, but does not say they sound one another out to obtain information.

astra-6.text:
I think the FOMO is quite strong, but we should distinguish between believing that AI is a major technological shift and believing that every AI investment is a good investment. Those are very different judgments.

For investors, the anxiety is understandable: if AI produces the next generation of major companies, missing them could be costly. But that anxiety can lead people to invest before they have a clear view of the product, the customers, or how the business will make money. A hot funding round can start to substitute for independent judgment.

The question I would ask is: if this company weren’t described as an AI company, would its customer value and business fundamentals still interest you? And as models become more capable and cheaper, does that strengthen the company’s advantage, or make its product easier to replicate?

You can be very optimistic about AI and still be disciplined about individual investments. In fact, the more important you think the opportunity is, the more carefully you should evaluate it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses strong FOMO, investment discipline, and business fundamentals, but does not say that investors sound one another out to obtain information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the FOMO is quite strong, but it’s uneven. Investors are worried about missing a major technological shift, so there’s pressure to invest before it’s clear which companies will build lasting businesses. That can make the fear of missing a deal outweigh the question of whether the price makes sense.

But enthusiasm for AI and the quality of a particular investment are two different things. AI can be transformative, and you can still lose money by investing at the wrong valuation or backing a company without a durable advantage.

For me, the useful question is: if you took “AI” out of the pitch, what would remain? Is there a real customer need? Do people keep using the product? Will they pay enough to support the business? FOMO becomes dangerous when those questions stop mattering.

r001.rationale: The response discusses strong, uneven FOMO and investment diligence, but does not say investors sound one another out to obtain information.
